title: Class 5 Maths Parts and Wholes: NCERT Chapter 4 Explained + Free Quiz
meta_title: Class 5 Maths Parts and Wholes (NCERT Ch 4)
meta_desc: Class 5 maths parts and wholes made simple: fractions of a whole and a collection, plus percentages, with real case studies and a free quiz.
excerpt: The Indian flag, a school garden, a restaurant bill — NCERT Chapter 4 hides fractions and percentages in things your child already sees. Here is how to teach Parts and Wholes so it finally makes sense, with two solved case studies and a quick quiz.
author: Sachin Sharma
content:
Hold up a photo of the Indian flag and ask a Class 5 child what fraction is orange. Most will say ‘one part’ before they say ‘one-third’. That small gap is exactly what the NCERT chapter on class 5 maths parts and wholes sets out to close — the idea that a whole splits into equal parts, and each part has a name, a number and, later, a percentage. Chapter 4 of the NCERT Class 5 Maths book (Math-Magic) does not teach fractions as cold sums. It hides them inside a flag, a garden bed, a chikki bar and a bill, and asks children to notice the parts.

I have taught this chapter to ten-year-olds in more than one Tier-2 city classroom, and the children who struggle are almost never bad at arithmetic. They just skipped one word: equal. Get that word right and the rest of the chapter falls into place.

What Parts and Wholes actually covers

The chapter moves through three connected ideas, in this order:

  • Fraction of a whole — one object cut into equal parts (a roti in 4, a flag in 3 bands).
  • Fraction of a collection — a group of separate things shared into equal shares (12 mangoes split so each child gets one-fourth).
  • Simple percentages — a special fraction with 100 as the whole, so half a pizza is also 50 out of 100, or 50%.

Notice that fractions of a collection trip up more children than fractions of a single object. A child happily shades half a rectangle, then freezes when asked for half of 8 laddoos. The fix is to physically share the group — count the whole, make equal piles, count one pile. That is the whole trick.

Fractions of a whole: start with the flag

The Indian flag is the friendliest example in the book because the three bands really are equal. Orange is one band out of three, so one-third. White is one-third. Green is one-third. Together, 1⁄3 + 1⁄3 + 1⁄3 makes 3⁄3, which is the whole flag — one. That last line, that the parts add back to one, is the single most important sentence in the chapter.

From there, folding paper beats any worksheet. Fold a strip once and you have halves; fold again and you have quarters; the crease lines make ‘equal’ visible instead of just spoken.

Fractions of a collection: sharing a group

Say a garden has 20 plants and one-fourth of them are tulsi. To find one-fourth of a collection, split the group into 4 equal shares and take one share: 20 ÷ 4 = 5 tulsi plants. Want three-fourths? Take three of those shares: 3 × 5 = 15. This is where fractions quietly start doing division and multiplication at the same time, which is why the chapter matters far beyond Class 5.

From fractions to percentages

Percentage is not a new monster; it is a fraction wearing a uniform. ‘Per cent’ means ‘out of a hundred’. So 1⁄2 = 50⁄100 = 50%, and 1⁄4 = 25⁄100 = 25%. To find a percentage of a quantity, turn the percent into a fraction and take that fraction of the amount.

Case study 1: the school garden

Read the passage the way the NCERT case-study format does, then answer in steps. Riya’s class plants a garden with 40 saplings. Half are neem, one-fourth are tulsi, and the rest are marigold.

  • How many neem? Half of 40 is 40 ÷ 2 = 20 neem.
  • How many tulsi? One-fourth of 40 is 40 ÷ 4 = 10 tulsi.
  • How many marigold? The rest = 40 − 20 − 10 = 10 marigold.
  • What percentage are marigold? 10 out of 40 is 10⁄40 = 1⁄4 = 25%.

One passage, four questions, three skills — fraction of a collection, subtraction to find the rest, and converting a fraction to a percentage. That layered style is exactly how the chapter is assessed.

Case study 2: the family bill

The Sharma family’s restaurant bill is ₹800. They add a 10% tip. A tip of 10% means 10 out of every 100 rupees, or 1⁄10 of the bill. So the tip is 800 ÷ 10 = ₹80, and the family pays 800 + 80 = ₹880. If instead a shop offered 25% off a ₹800 item, the discount would be one-fourth of 800 = ₹200, leaving ₹600. Same chapter, opposite direction — and both come up constantly once children start noticing prices.

A common mistake to watch for

Children often write the wrong ‘whole’. Asked for one-third of a flag, they answer ‘3’ because they see three bands, forgetting that one-third means one of those three. Always ask two questions in order: how many equal parts in all, and how many are we taking? Whole first, then the part.

Try the quiz, then the case-study practice

The short quiz below covers fractions of a whole, fractions of a collection and simple percentages — the exact spread of this NCERT chapter. Let your child attempt all eight, then read the explanations together for any misses. quiz.title: Class 5 Parts and Wholes Quiz
quiz.intro: Eight questions on fractions of a whole, fractions of a collection and simple percentages, straight from NCERT Chapter 4. Pick an answer for each, then press Check my score.
quiz.about: NCERT Class 5 Maths Chapter 4: Parts and Wholes

questions.q: The Indian flag has three equal bands. What fraction is the orange band?
questions.explanation: Three equal bands means each band is one out of three, so the orange band is one-third.

questions.q: A roti is cut into 4 equal pieces and you eat 3. What fraction did you eat?
questions.explanation: Three of the four equal pieces is 3⁄4.

questions.q: A garden has 20 plants. One-fourth are tulsi. How many tulsi plants?
questions.explanation: One-fourth of a collection means split into 4 equal shares: 20 ÷ 4 = 5.

questions.q: Which percentage is the same as one-half?
questions.explanation: One-half is 50 out of 100, which is 50%.
Three thirds make 3⁄3, which is the whole, equal to one.

questions.q: A bar of chocolate is shared so 25% is left. What fraction is left?
questions.explanation: 25% means 25 out of 100, which simplifies to one-fourth.

questions.q: There are 12 mangoes. Three-fourths are ripe. How many are ripe?
questions.explanation: One-fourth of 12 is 3, so three-fourths is 3 × 3 = 9.

faq.q: What is the NCERT Class 5 Maths Chapter 4 Parts and Wholes about?
faq.a: It teaches fractions of a whole (like the three equal bands of the flag), fractions of a collection (sharing a group of objects into equal shares), and simple percentages of a quantity, all through real examples such as gardens, bills and food.

faq.q: Why do children find fractions of a collection harder than fractions of a shape?
faq.a: Shading half a shape looks obvious, but finding half of 8 objects needs a child to count the whole group, make equal piles and count one pile. Sharing real objects — buttons, coins, laddoos — fixes this quickly.

faq.q: How do you explain percentages to a Class 5 student?
faq.a: A percentage is just a fraction with 100 as the whole. ‘Per cent’ means ‘out of a hundred’, so one-half is 50 out of 100, or 50%. To find a percentage of an amount, turn the percent into a fraction and take that fraction of the amount.

faq.q: What is the most common mistake in this chapter?
faq.a: Forgetting the word ‘equal’ and confusing the whole with the part. Asked for one-third of a flag, some children answer ‘3’ instead of ‘1 of 3’. Always ask how many equal parts in all, then how many you are taking.
